q: 1. Unevenness of a pavement should be preferably less than .............
explain: An unevenness index of less than 150 cm/km is considered good for high-speed roads, while values above 250 cm/km indicate poor riding quality.

q: 2. Skidding occurs on ............. pavement.
explain: Skidding occurs when the pavement surface is smooth or slippery (low friction), causing the wheels to slide without rotating.

q: 3. The layer of the road that may not contribute to unevenness is.
explain: The formation is the prepared natural ground. Unevenness is usually a result of poor construction or settlement of the artificial pavement layers above it.

q: 4. A drawback of a rigid pavement is that .............
options: no crack occurs even if local settlement takes place
it acts as a bridge to cover minor depression like irregularity
its ability to withstand iron wheeled traffic is less
explain: Rigid pavements are brittle; once a structural crack (rift) starts due to fatigue or temperature, it tends to propagate and widen quickly.

q: 5. An example of a rigid pavement is .............
explain: Cement concrete roads are the classic example of rigid pavements, where the slab itself provides structural strength through flexural rigidity.

q: 6. When lime is added to a soil, it .............
options: increases grain size due to electrolytic and chemical action
lowers plastic limit and increases liquid limit
explain: Lime causes flocculation of clay particles, effectively increasing the apparent grain size and making the soil more workable.

q: 7. Surface painting is .............
options: marking of white and yellow lines on pavement
providing a thin Bituminous layer over WBM roads
application of Bitumen concrete layer over WBM roads
application of a hot mix of bitumen and then stone chips over it
explain: Also known as surface dressing, it involves spraying hot bitumen followed by a layer of stone chips to provide a wearing surface.

q: 8. A Bitumen Bound Macadam Pavement is best suited where .............
options: ground water table is at shallow depths
the climate is hot and humid
explain: Bitumen Bound Macadam (BBM) is an open-graded premix; it performs best in dry regions (scant rainfall) where drainage through the layer is less of a concern.

q: 9. Minimum lateral clearance desirable from the pavement edge is .............
explain: For safety and capacity, objects (like poles or trees) should ideally be at least 1.85m away from the edge of the traveled lane.

q: 10. A lamp post at the edge of the pavement reduces the capacity of the lane to .............
explain: Obstacles near the lane edge cause 'lateral clearance' effects where drivers slow down or move away, reducing overall lane capacity to about 83%.

q: 11. Full amount of extra width of a pavement on the curve, is provided at
explain: Widening is introduced gradually along the transition curve and reaches its full value at the start of the circular curve.

q: 12. In case of cement concrete pavements, pick up the incorrect statement
options: initial cost of construction is high
initial cost of construction is low
explain: Concrete pavements are known for having a high initial construction cost compared to flexible (bituminous) pavements.

q: 13. The basic formula for determination of pavement thickness was first suggested by
explain: Goldbeck provided early simplified formulas for pavement thickness based on wheel loads and allowable stresses.

q: 14. When each particle of aggregates is thinly coated with cement paste, a heterogeneous solid is formed, which is known as
explain: Concrete is a composite material formed by binding aggregates (sand/gravel) together with cement paste.

q: 15. If d is the economic designed depth of a slab, the thickness of the cement concrete pavement slab at interior, is kept
explain: The interior of the slab experiences less stress than the corners/edges, so the thickness can be reduced to roughly 85% of the edge thickness.

q: 16. Minimum thickness of a layer of fine sand required to cut off capillary rise of water completely, should be
explain: To completely break the capillary attraction in fine-grained soils, a thick sand blanket of about 76 cm is required.

q: 17. To prevent movement of moisture from subgrade to road pavement at the same level as that of water-table, thickness of a cut off layer of coarse sand, is
explain: Coarse sand has larger voids, making a thinner layer (15 cm) effective as a capillary cut-off compared to fine sand.

q: 18. Newly constructed pavement with ordinary Portland cement attains its working strength after
explain: Concrete is traditionally considered to have reached its full design strength at the 28-day curing mark.

q: 19. Pavement is said to be flexible if it contains
explain: Flexible pavements are those that deform under load and transmit pressure through grain-to-grain contact; WBM and bitumen layers fit this description.

q: 20. Design of flexible pavement, involves
explain: Designers must consider the magnitude of load, frequency of application (traffic), and environmental factors like rainfall and temperature.

q: 21. Design of flexible pavements is based on
options: a compromise of pure theory and empirical formula
explain: Most flexible pavement design methods (like CBR) are based on empirical observations and testing rather than rigid structural theory.

q: 22. California Bearing Ratio method of designing flexible pavements is more accurate as it involves
options: character of the road making materials
explain: The CBR test directly measures the resistance of the subgrade soil to penetration, which is the primary factor in flexible pavement thickness.

q: 23. Cement grouted pavement is classified as
explain: Because it uses a cement binder within a stone matrix but doesn't have the full structural slab action of PCC, it is called semi-rigid.

q: 24. Design of highways is based on
explain: Pavement structural design is primarily governed by the weight transmitted through the axle loads (e.g., the 8160 kg standard axle).

q: 25. On most smooth hard surfaced roads, rolling resistance to moving vehicles, ranges from
explain: For standard hard pavements, the rolling resistance typically falls within the 9 to 11 kg per tonne range.

q: 26. The top of the ground on which the foundation of road rests, is called ............
explain: The sub-grade is the naturally occurring or prepared soil bed that supports the entire pavement structure.

q: 27. The thickness of road surfacing depends upon the ............
explain: Pavement thickness design considers the load (type/intensity of traffic) and the structural properties of the materials used.

q: 28. The shape of the camber provided for cement concrete pavement is ............
explain: Straight-line cambers are preferred for concrete pavements because they are easier to construct and maintain with rigid slabs.

q: 29. A water bound macadam road is an example of ............
explain: WBM (Water Bound Macadam) consists of crushed stone layers held together by water and stone dust; it behaves as a flexible pavement.

q: 30. A cement grouted road is an example of ............ pavement.
explain: Cement grouted pavements have higher stiffness than flexible ones but less than a full RC slab, classifying them as semi-rigid.

q: 31. The flexible pavement distribute the wheel load ............
options: through a set of layers to sub-grade
explain: Flexible pavements distribute loads through grain-to-grain contact across various layers (surface, base, sub-base) down to the sub-grade.

q: 32. The natural soil on which the pavement rests and to which the entire load of structure is ultimately transferred, is known as the ............
explain: The sub-grade is the bottom-most layer consisting of natural or compacted soil that bears the total load of the road.

q: 33. The sub-base course is placed immediately above the ............
explain: The sub-base is the layer directly on top of the sub-grade soil.

q: 34. The selection of design curve in Wyoming method of flexible pavement design, is based upon ............
explain: The Wyoming method uses a chart-based design that adjusts for climate factors like rainfall, water table depth, and frost.

q: 35. The group index method of designing flexible pavement is ............
options: an empirical method based on the physical properties of the sub-grades soil
an empirical method based on the strength characteristics of the sub-grade soil
explain: The Group Index (GI) is calculated using soil properties like liquid limit, plasticity index, and the percentage passing the 75-micron sieve.

q: 36. The value of group index of a soil varies from ............
explain: The Group Index formula yields values between 0 (very good sub-grade) and 20 (very poor sub-grade).

q: 37. The longitudinal joints may be ............
explain: Various joint designs are used in concrete construction to ensure load transfer or to provide a controlled plane of weakness for cracking.

q: 38. The longitudinal joint in concrete pavements, as recommended by I.R.C., is of ............
explain: IRC recommends the use of tied or hinged joints for longitudinal purposes to keep the slabs from separating while allowing for rotation.

q: 39. To prevent the development of excessive compressive stresses in the concrete pavements as a result of expansion caused by increase in temperature, the type of transverse joint provided is ............
explain: Expansion joints contain a compressible filler material that allows concrete slabs to expand during hot weather without crushing each other.

q: 40. The dowel bars are used in rigid pavements for ............
options: transferring load from one portion to another
explain: Dowel bars are smooth steel bars placed across transverse joints to transfer wheel loads from one slab to the next, ensuring smooth transitions.

q: 41. Transverse contraction joints relieve ............ stresses in concrete.
explain: Concrete is weak in tension. Contraction joints allow the slab to shorten during cooling or drying, relieving the internal tensile stresses that cause cracking.
